rows.en: The meeting of various events, one with another, in the life of these sages bore and caused to sprout a division of opinions even among the Pharisees. This division was indeed small at the beginning of its appearance, but not many days passed and it became like a swelling spring. The ordinance that they enacted to limit the number of expounders was for the good as to its intention, but as to the consequences that came out of it, it was not a blessing. It is not possible that the expounders of the Torah, before whom the doors of their house of study were shut, ceased entirely from expounding the Torah; rather, they expounded and expounded in other places. Already after the death of Shemaiah and Avtalyon two men stood at the head of the Sanhedrin, namely the sons of Betera, who were not among those who came to their house of study (Pesaḥim 66a, and Yerushalmi there). It is further told that against the halakhah that when the Passover falls on the Sabbath the festival offering [ḥagigah] is not offered with it, two sages of that generation protested, namely Judah ben Durtai and his son Durtai, and they separated from the sages and went and settled in the South. For they said: “If Elijah comes and says to Israel, ‘Why did you not offer the festival offering on the Sabbath?’, what will they say to him? I wonder at the two great men of the generation, Shemaiah and Avtalyon, who are great sages and great expounders, and did not tell Israel that the festival offering overrides the Sabbath” (Bavli there 70a⚠1). From this we learn that Judah and his son were not among the disciples of Shemaiah and Avtalyon, and the ways of their midrash were not pleasing in their eyes. And it is possible that already in those days there were houses of Torah in the South. And of the sons of Betera it is told that once, when they were heads of the Sanhedrin, it happened that the eve of Passover fell on the Sabbath, and they forgot and did not know whether the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath. They said: “There is a certain man, Hillel the Babylonian is his name, who came up from Babylonia, and he served the two great men of the generation, Shemaiah and Avtalyon, and he knows whether the Passover overrides the Sabbath.” And Hillel expounded to them by the rules [middot] by which the Torah is expounded, to bring proof that the Passover overrides the Sabbath, and they did not accept it from him until he said: “Thus I received it from Shemaiah and Avtalyon.” From this we see that they did not want midrash by the rules, but they were satisfied when they heard from the mouth of Hillel that the halakhah in question was received by him from Shemaiah and Avtalyon. From the combination of these events we understand that in the days of Shemaiah and Avtalyon they began to pave new paths in the exposition of the Torah, and these two heads were described by the title of honor “great expounders”; in the first generation after them a beginning was made to set an order and a number for the rules and to give them names. All this shows that the new paths that they paved for themselves were in the domain of the midrash of the Torah, and this innovation met with opponents among the Pharisees. And since we have no other reason for this innovation except the effort of the Pharisees to strike the crown of the head of the Sadducees and to give the opinions of the Pharisees a foundation and a root in the Written Torah, we must judge from this that the opponents among the Pharisees also refused to accept the widening of the midrash of the Torah by the rules. And now it is clear that at that time the division of opinions among the Pharisees themselves began; and by this we understand how already in the generation after this the small division became a great dispute among the sages, until they said that because of the dispute the Torah became like two Torahs.

1.note: The story of Judah ben Durtai is in Pesaḥim 70b; kept as printed (70a).

rows.en: But the new paths that Shemaiah and Avtalyon paved in the midrash of the Torah were desolate after their death. The opponents raised their heads, for from their midst the sons of Betera were chosen and set up to sit at the head of the Sanhedrin. According to what is told in the Talmud about them, they were poor in wisdom, so much so that they forgot and did not know a simple halakhah (there 66a, and in the Yerushalmi at the beginning of ch. 6). The later sages said of their time that it was a time of the forgetting of the Torah (Sukkah 20a), and in the Mishnah in which the chain of the receivers of the tradition is mentioned, the sons of Betera have no name or mention (Avot 1:1). The matter of the sons of Betera will become much clearer to us when we come to the story of the life of Hillel the Babylonian. But on one thing we must set our heart here, namely: it is very surprising how men who were not distinguished in wisdom reached the highest rank in the nation with respect to its religious affairs. However, we shall understand this phenomenon if we set our eyes on the course of the history of the nations in the world since ancient times. From of old it has been so, that when the wheel of government turns, almost always men without a name are raised up, while the good among the people hide or are brought to ruin before those who oppress them. So too it was when Herod seized the government with a strong hand: in all the offices that he filled, ability and excellence of wisdom were not his line and plummet; rather the man who humbled himself under his feet and called good whatever he called good, he was the man whom he wished to raise to the top. So too we saw when he raised Ḥanamel the Egyptian to be high priest, although this priest was not among the great ones of the priests and was not counted among men of name (*Antiquities* 15, 2; Parah 3); and this was only because he knew that this man, who was of the poor of the people, would be his servant and would bend to whatever he wished. And this too was the reason why he set the sons of Betera as heads of the Sanhedrin: he hoped that they would be in his hand like clay in the hand of the potter. But the days came when they themselves recognized that they did not have the power to fill the office over which they had been set, and then with a willing soul they made room for a man who was loved and favored by the people and whose fame went through all the land.

Now if we cast a glance over the days of the long period that we have passed through so far, we find that with all the hardships and troubles that befell the nation and the sages, their hands did not slacken from the Torah, but they held fast to it. They expounded the Torah and interpreted it according to their way, and they also had many traditional interpretations in their hands. In the course of this time hearts were divided and a difference of opinions arose. On the ground of religion two ways were most prominent, namely: the way of the Pharisees and the way of the Sadducees. The Pharisees chose for themselves a way that goes forward in widening the interpretation of the Torah, and the Sadducees went backward from the time that their heart was divided and they turned aside from the way of the Pharisees. At all times the Pharisees roused themselves to stand against the Sadducees and to subdue them. At various times the war was heavy and victory changed ten times: at one time the Pharisees stood at the head and at another the Sadducees, until in the end the Pharisees defeated the Sadducees with a lasting victory. For this reason they fixed firm rules, and made amendments and statutes in order to make a public stand against the Sadducees, and they did so even when they were forced to uproot words of the Torah, because the hour required it. This reason was before their eyes in every matter and in every way. Therefore they were not strict about departing from the words of their predecessors, even when these were founded in the Torah, where the need of the hour and the strengthening⚠1 of the Torah as a whole required it. They tried to strengthen their teachings by bringing proofs for them from the Written Torah according to the ways of their midrash. They had known rules for the purpose of interpreting the Torah from of old, and these were called the rules [middot] by which the Torah is expounded. These rules, which the later sages divided into various numbers, they widened, and in proportion to their widening the interpretations also widened. The consequences that came out of the interpretations became fixed halakhot. So too they made ordinances, fences and decrees as their time had need of them. And when they fixed all these, they did not fix them in storm and dispute but by the consent of the Sanhedrin. But the fact that they widened the Torah too much because of the opposition of the Sadducees already caused, at the end of the period, a slight opposition among the Pharisees too, and the agreement among them was disturbed. This opposition was at its beginning like one who lets out water [Proverbs 17:14], and in the next generation it became a flowing river that had no restraint any more in all the generations to come. Since the events grew mighty upon them and the hardships increased exceedingly, therefore the forgetting of the Torah also grew time after time. So we saw in the days of Yose ben Yoezer that some of the halakhic statutes needed Yose's testimony, because they had been forgotten in his time; also the decrees that Yose ben Yoezer and his colleague decreed were forgotten after a time, until Simeon ben Shetaḥ restored them. After the death of Yose ben Yoezer the “clusters” [eshkolot] ceased, and the Torah was forgotten in the days of the wars. And at the time that the Sadducees stood at the head, the forgetting of the Torah also grew, until they said of that time that the world was desolate until Simeon ben Shetaḥ came (Kiddushin 66a). And did not Judah ben Tabbai his colleague, although he stood at the head of the Sanhedrin, nonetheless have a great halakhah hidden from him, and a mishap came about through him, for innocent blood was shed? And again in the days of the sons of Betera the teaching of the Pharisees was forsaken, and there was no man in Jerusalem who remained of the survivors of the disciples of Shemaiah and Avtalyon; and this is a clear sign of how little the Torah was expounded in the way that Shemaiah and Avtalyon held. But this last forgetting was the reason that the exposition of the Torah reached a new stage.

1.note: Last word of p. 145; its final letter is blurred (ת or ה). Read והחזקת, 'and the strengthening of'.

rows.en: Hillel, Menaḥem, Shammai; their way in the midrash of the Torah and in the halakhah; Akavya ben Mahalalel; the House of Shammai; the House of Hillel; Simeon the son of Hillel; Rabban Gamaliel the Elder and the sages of his generation; Simeon his son and the sages of his generation.

The good forces were weakened by the rod of Herod. The upheaval that he brought about in all the affairs of the nation worked very much for the worse also on the exposition of the Torah. For from the first day that he came to the throne, terror came with him; the peace of the sages passed away and agitation came in its place. Shemaiah and Avtalyon, in the strength of their spirit, still stood in the breach; but when they died, quiet and security died with them, and the light of the exposition of the Torah no longer shone as before, and darkness could be felt [Exodus 10:21]. This darkness was doubled further on account of the division of opinions that broke out among the sages of the Pharisees. And the end of all this was that the time came of the lack of exposition and of the forgetting of the Oral Torah. At this time there came up, like a root out of a dry ground [Isaiah 53:2], a man wonderful in his wisdom and in honorable qualities, and he reached the seat of the patriarchate. This man was Hillel the Babylonian, who is also called Hillel the Elder. His descent was from a high family in Israel. His father was of the tribe of Benjamin and his mother of the root of Jesse the Bethlehemite, of the descendants of Shephatiah son of King David and his wife Abital (Yerushalmi Kil'ayim ch. 9). His native land was Babylonia, and therefore he was called Hillel the Babylonian (Pesaḥim 66a; Sukkah 20a). The year of his birth was around the end of the seventh century of the fourth millennium.{v1_09_02:1} He had a brother named Shebna, who engaged in trade, and Hillel did not want to be his partner in his trade, for his soul desired the Torah, and he parted from him (Sotah 21a) and went to Jerusalem to hear Torah from the mouth of Shemaiah and Avtalyon. From this it appears that at that time there were no houses of Torah in Babylonia. True, in the days of the exile the Torah was planted in Babylonia; also the men who brought it back to the Land of Israel and planted it there were Babylonians who returned “when the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion” [Psalms 126:1]. But these days were not like the former days, for the times had changed, and the exposition of the Torah had now come to a new stage, and this stage depended on the Land of Israel, where most of the halakhot and midrashim were born. Likewise the ordinances and decrees arose from events that happened there and from the needs of the time in the land of their dwelling. In addition to this, all the days of the Temple there was no man of Israel who did not hold with complete faith to the great principle “for out of Zion shall go forth the Torah” [Isaiah 2:3], and any matter of halakhah, midrash or fence that had not been voted on and concluded in the Great Court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone did not have binding force for them. Therefore it is self-evident that in Babylonia there was no place for the exposition of the Torah, nor could there be. Nor has anything great or small reached us of the exposition of the Torah among the Babylonian Jews; we are only told that they followed the customs of the Jews and were very strict in keeping the Sabbath, and sent their shekels and their offerings and gifts to Jerusalem; but of a spread of Torah study among them there is no hint at all. A hint to the matter, that the exposition of the Torah in Babylonia at that time was only small, is given us by the story told of Izates (Zotos in the Midrash Rabbah⚠1), king of Adiabene, who entered the Jewish religion with his mother and sent his sons to Jerusalem to study Torah (Josephus, *Antiquities* 20), although Babylonia was near to him. And from the continuation of that story another difference appears between the views of the Jerusalemites and of the Babylonians. For it is further told there that the teacher of Izates, who taught him the law of the Jews, was a Jew from his own country named Ḥananiah; and when the teacher and his pupil took counsel together about the necessity of circumcision, Ḥananiah permitted the king to accept the Jewish religion without circumcising the flesh of his foreskin, for he said that it is possible to worship God even while uncircumcised, if only he cleaves to the law of the Jews with a whole heart. Not so thought another Jewish sage from the land of Galilee, called by the name Eleazar, for he told the king that it is not enough to know the ways of God and His laws, but he must keep His commandments, and circumcision is a duty from which there is no exemption in any way. From this it appears that the Babylonian did not make the deed the main thing, and certainly the Babylonians were not strict in the details of the practical commandments as the people of the Land of Israel were; and this too is some proof that in Babylonia they were not strict in the details of the Torah and of the Scribes as the Jerusalemites were. And who knows whether it was not this laxity that caused the Babylonians to be hated by the people of the Land of Israel, so that every frivolous thing (Yoma 66b), and likewise every improper deed by the measure of proper conduct, they ascribed to the Babylonians (Menaḥot 100a). And it is a clear fact that at that time the Babylonians were regarded in the eyes of the people of the Land of Israel as not knowing the Torah. For only in this way can we understand the saying of the sons of Betera, who said — when Hillel expounded before them to bring proof that the Passover overrides the Sabbath — “We have already said: is there any hope from a Babylonian?” (Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1). And it is no empty thing that the Babylonian Gemara omitted this saying from the baraita, and always strives to show the strength of the Babylonians in the Torah, and that at all times they were the men who brought the Torah to the Land of Israel; this is only because the reverse was well known among the people of the Land of Israel. But the effort of the later sages to show that it was not so did not help them, and their testimony is contradicted by reality. For what does it help when they say that in the days of Ezra the Torah was forgotten and he brought it up with him from Babylonia? This is still no decisive proof that the exposition, as it developed from the days of Ezra to the days of Hillel, found a place for itself in Babylonia. And what more does it help if they boast that Hillel was a Babylonian and that he founded the Torah anew in the Land of Israel at the time when it had been forgotten, since it is a clear fact that Hillel did not bring all his Torah and his wisdom from his country, but rather he went to the Land of Israel to expound the Torah? Therefore Hillel did not bring the Torah from Babylonia; rather it was the reverse: he went up to the Land of Israel and studied there, and returned to Babylonia and brought the Torah with him, and perhaps he was the first who began to rouse the heart of his Babylonian countrymen to the exposition of the Torah. And in the days of the last war that the Jews had with the Romans, some of the sages escaped for their lives and went down to Babylonia or to Aram (Mesopotamia) near it, such as R. Judah ben Betera, who settled in Nisibis in Aram; and without doubt other sages went down there too; and likewise after the destruction sages of the Land of Israel settled there, such as Ḥananiah the nephew of R. Joshua. Therefore from the time of Hillel onward the exposition of the Torah was brought to Babylonia by various sages from the Land of Israel.

1.note: במ"ר read as 'in the Midrash Rabbah'; the sons of Ptolemy, Monobaz and Zotos, appear in Genesis Rabbah 46.

rows.en: The days of Hillel's stay in the Land of Israel, while he was serving his masters, were bad; there he lived a life of distress and sustained his soul by the labor of his hands. He was a day laborer and the wage of his work was small; but since he was modest in all his wants, this little sufficed him for his needs and more. From the surplus he paid the doorkeeper of the house of study of Shemaiah and Avtalyon half the tropaic [coin] that was due to him according to the custom in force. One day Hillel earned nothing and could not pay his due; but this did not keep him from hearing Torah, for instead of going inside into the house of study, he went and lay down at the opening of the skylight to hear from there the teaching of his masters. That night much snow fell to the ground, until all his body was covered to a height of three cubits. In the morning the day did not grow light as before, and all who sat in the house of study wondered; the matter was sought and found, and behold, the body of a man lay at the opening of the skylight, covered with snow. They quickly removed him from there, and behold, it was Hillel. They washed him, anointed him and sat him opposite the fire, and said: this one is worthy that the Sabbath be profaned for him (Yoma 35b). So strong was the love of the Torah within him. But as he loved the wisdom of the Torah, so he loved all the other sciences and inquired into them. They said of him that he left no matter of the words of wisdom that he did not learn: he studied foreign languages and all kinds of sciences; all of it he learned in order to magnify the Torah and make it glorious [Isaiah 42:21] (Soferim ch. 16). In this way too he guided his disciples, and taught them to hold fast to the Torah and not to let their hands go from the other sciences (Sukkah 28a; Bava Batra 139a⚠1). His love for the exposition of the Torah is seen especially from his leaving the land of his birth and going to a land that at that time was full of strife and horror. But he saw that in Babylonia he could not fulfill his longing; and even if he expounded by himself or in the company of sages in his country, he knew well that, according to the state of the wisdom of the Torah at that time in the Land of Israel, from which instruction goes forth, he could not attain what he sought. For if he expounded and drew halakhic consequences from his expositions, he still did not know whether his exposition agreed with the halakhah that was the practice of the people and had been agreed upon in the Great Court in Jerusalem. And this is the thing that moved him to go up to the Land of Israel. Indeed it is told that Hillel went up from Babylonia on account of three matters. The first was the matter of the purity and impurity of the leper (Sifra Tazria ch. 10). The second was the eating of matzah from the new grain. And the third was the festival offering (Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1). In these three matters the halakhah was in doubt for him, and there was no man in Babylonia who could resolve his doubts, for they did not know how these had been decided by the court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and how the matters were practiced in the custom of the people in Jerusalem. And if they said that he went up on account of three matters, without doubt this is not exact; rather he had doubts already before this, but he still delayed leaving his country and his birthplace until doubts came to him in these three matters; then his soul was strengthened to go up to Jerusalem, and he went up. Nor was his hope disappointed, for in truth he expounded, reached agreement, went up and received the halakhah (Yerushalmi there). The same happened to other sages who lived in Babylonia: they expounded according to the ways of analogy and thought that their midrash was founded on foundations of truth which all the winds in the world could not move from their place, and nonetheless they were forced to set aside their opinion and to overturn their analogy and their midrash, because it had not been so decided in the Great Court in Jerusalem, and the halakhah was the opposite of what they had derived by their midrash. So it happened at a later time, close to the destruction of the Temple or right after it, to one of the sages who went down to Nisibis, namely R. Judah ben Betera. This sage too derived a midrashic consequence and set up the halakhah that a betrothed daughter of Israel eats terumah, and he proved this by the rule of kal va-ḥomer. Then a sage, one of his friends, named Yoḥanan ben Bag Bag, sent to him as if in wonder, saying: “They said in your name that a betrothed daughter of Israel eats terumah!” He sent back and said to him: “I held you to be expert in the secrets of the Torah; you do not know even how to expound a kal va-ḥomer!” And he expounded a kal va-ḥomer before him, but he added, saying: “And what shall I do, when they said: a woman never eats terumah until she enters the bridal canopy, and they supported it with the verse ‘every one that is clean in thy house shall eat of it’ [Numbers 18:11]” (Yerushalmi and Tosefta Ketubbot ch. 5; and see Kiddushin 10b; Sifrei Koraḥ sec. 117). Thus we see that what happened to Hillel happened to him, except that Hillel expounded, reached agreement and received the halakhah, while he expounded and derived a consequence from his midrash, and although he had no reason to overturn his midrash on its scholarly side, he was forced to overturn it because the custom in the Land of Israel in his time was the opposite of the consequence of his midrash. For in truth the ancient halakhah agreed with his midrash, for at first they said that a betrothed daughter of Israel eats terumah, and they derived this from Scripture, and a later court decided the opposite and derived the opposite also from Scripture (Yerushalmi there). Therefore it is self-evident that the midrash of R. Judah ben Betera too could not stand against the decision of the court in the Land of Israel.{v1_09_04:1} And now we understand how hard it was for the expounders in Babylonia to decide a matter as halakhah and for practice, which has no standing if there is no agreement on it from the court in Jerusalem; therefore it is not surprising that Hillel chose to live in Jerusalem to learn Torah from Shemaiah and Avtalyon. We cannot fix with certainty the days of his service to his masters, but it appears that he returned once more to his country: the first time he went up to Jerusalem to satisfy his longing to learn Torah from Shemaiah and Avtalyon, and then he did not go up at the request of the sages of the Land of Israel, by their wish to ask halakhah of him (commentary of Rabad to the Sifra, at its beginning); rather he received halakhah from them, not they from him. After a time, and this without doubt at the time when Herod persecuted the sages, he returned to his country; but when the land was quiet he came back once more to Jerusalem, and this return was before the hallowing of the Feast of Unleavened Bread [Isaiah 30:29]. When all Israel gathered in Jerusalem to sacrifice the Passover sacrifice, Hillel too was among those who came.

1.note: Hillel's disciples are in Bava Batra 134a; printed קל"ט (139), kept as printed.

footnotes.en: In the Sifrei, at its end, we learn: Hillel came up from Babylonia at forty years of age, served [the sages] forty years, and led Israel forty years. And in Shabbat (15a) they said: Hillel held his patriarchate before the Temple [was destroyed] a hundred years. According to the Sifrei he became patriarch at eighty years of age, and was born in the year 3650 of the world. Now when he came up from Babylonia he was already a sage, for he expounded, reached agreement and received the halakhah (Sifra Tazria ch. 10; Tosefta Nega'im ch. 1; Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1). If he had lived there forty years and served, how is it that the patriarchs did not know of him? And in Pesaḥim it is proved that they did not recognize him, and one of the disciples hinted at him and said: “There is a certain man, Hillel the Babylonian is his name.” But it is true that the number in the Sifrei is not exact. And it appears that in his youth he went up to the Land of Israel to learn Torah from Shemaiah and Avtalyon; and perhaps at the time that Herod persecuted the sages he returned to his country, and after the land was quiet he came back once to the Land of Israel for some reason, and then it came about that he became patriarch, as told in the text. And it is possible that he became patriarch at forty years of age and led Israel forty years; according to this all the days of his life were eighty years, as Graetz fixed his time, vol. 3, p. 207. Therefore, if he became patriarch a hundred years before the destruction, and lived eighty years and led Israel forty years, then the year of his birth falls a hundred and forty years before the destruction, which is the year 3690 of the world. But in truth there is no proof by which we can fix the year of his birth with complete exactness, for we do not know clearly the exact number of the days of his life; therefore I have estimated his time only approximately, not exactly.
